points.title: Variables and fair tests
points.brief: In a fair test you change one variable (independent), measure one (dependent) and keep the rest the same (controlled), and repeat trials so results are reliable. An observational study watches without changing anything.

points.title: Observations and inferences
points.brief: An observation is what you see or measure. An inference is an explanation you draw from observations, which further tests can support or reject.

points.title: Measuring with instruments
points.brief: Choosing the right instrument and unit for length, mass, volume and temperature, and how digital and analog instruments compare in range and sensitivity, and with our senses.

points.title: Graphs and conclusions
points.brief: Column graphs suit categories and line graphs suit measured values that change, and a conclusion says what the trend in the data shows about the aim.

points.title: Theories and laws
points.brief: A scientific law describes a pattern that always happens. A theory explains why, using a large body of evidence from many scientists, and both can change when new evidence appears.

points.title: Scientific models
points.brief: A model, such as a diagram, a physical model or a computer simulation, represents something real using data. It helps explain and predict, but leaves some things out.

points.title: Data and data science
points.brief: Data science uses data, methods and computers to find patterns. Our online activity creates data about us too, so we need to share it carefully.

points.title: Models of the solar system
points.brief: The Earth-centred model was replaced by the Sun-centred model when new evidence, such as Galileo's telescope observations, did not fit the old one.

points.title: Phases of the Moon
points.brief: The Moon reflects sunlight, and as it orbits Earth over about a month we see different amounts of its lit half, from new moon to full moon.

points.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
points.brief: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomy
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have long linked the Moon's phases to the tides, and used the positions of stars, such as the Emu in the Sky, to know when seasons, weather and animal behaviour would change.

points.title: Contact and non-contact forces
points.brief: Contact forces, such as friction and a push, act where objects touch. Non-contact forces, such as gravity and magnetism, act at a distance.

points.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
points.brief: Force arrows show the size and direction of each force. Balanced forces leave motion unchanged, and unbalanced forces make an object speed up, slow down or change direction.

points.title: Mass and weight
points.brief: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity on it, in newtons, found with weight equals mass times gravitational acceleration.

points.title: Magnetic poles
points.brief: Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract, and the force gets weaker with distance.

points.title: Magnetic fields
points.brief: A magnetic field is the area around a magnet where its force acts, shown by field lines running from north to south that are closest where the field is strongest.

points.title: Electromagnets
points.brief: A current in a coil of wire makes a magnet that can be switched off. More turns, more current or an iron core make it stronger.

points.title: Levers and pulleys
points.brief: Simple machines such as levers and pulleys change the size or direction of a force, so a smaller effort can move a larger load.

points.title: Characteristics of living things
points.brief: Living things move, respire, are sensitive to their surroundings, grow, reproduce, excrete wastes and need nutrition.

points.title: Levels of classification
points.brief: Scientists sort organisms into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, and name each with a two-part scientific name, its genus and species.

points.title: Dichotomous keys
points.brief: A dichotomous key identifies an organism through a series of questions, each with two choices about a visible feature, until only one name is left.

points.title: Adaptations
points.brief: Structural, behavioural and physiological adaptations help organisms survive in their habitat, such as how Australian animals and plants cope with heat and little water.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander classification
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples classify plants and animals by their uses, forms and functions, a system built on deep knowledge of Country.

points.title: Cell theory and the microscope
points.brief: All living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells. Microscopes let us see them.

points.title: Plant and animal cells
points.brief: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria. Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Mitochondria release energy and chloroplasts make food.

points.title: Bacterial and fungal cells
points.brief: Bacterial cells are small and have no nucleus. Fungal cells have a nucleus and a cell wall but no chloroplasts.

points.title: Specialised cells, tissues and organs
points.brief: In many-celled organisms, cells take on special shapes for special jobs, such as nerve and red blood cells. Similar cells form tissues, and tissues form organs.

points.title: The digestive system
points.brief: The mouth, stomach and intestines break food down into small molecules that pass into the blood, and wastes leave the body.

points.title: The circulatory and respiratory systems
points.brief: The lungs take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and the heart pumps blood through blood vessels to carry these gases and nutrients to and from every cell.

points.title: The excretory system
points.brief: The kidneys filter wastes from the blood to make urine, which the bladder stores, and the skin and lungs also remove wastes.

points.title: Body systems working together
points.brief: Body systems depend on each other, so damage to one organ or system, such as a blocked artery, affects other systems and the whole body.

points.title: Plant transport and support
points.brief: Roots take up water and minerals, xylem carries water up the plant, phloem carries sugars from the leaves, and stems hold the plant up.

points.title: Biotic and abiotic factors
points.brief: An ecosystem is made of living (biotic) parts, such as plants and animals, and non-living (abiotic) parts, such as water, light and soil, that affect each other.

points.title: Food chains, webs and energy pyramids
points.brief: Energy passes from producers to consumers along food chains, and only a small part passes up each level, so an energy pyramid narrows towards the top. Decomposers return matter to the soil.

points.title: Introduced species
points.brief: A species brought into an ecosystem, such as the cane toad or the European rabbit, can change populations of native species by competing with, eating or poisoning them.

points.title: Threatened species in Australia
points.brief: Habitat loss, introduced species, disease and climate change make species vulnerable or endangered, and Australia has one of the world's highest rates of mammal extinction.

points.title: The particle model
points.brief: Solids, liquids and gases are made of particles. In solids they are held tightly and vibrate in place, in liquids they slide past each other, and in gases they move freely and far apart.

points.title: Changes of state
points.brief: Melting, freezing, evaporating, boiling and condensing happen as particles gain or lose energy, and the temperature stays level on a heating graph while the state changes.

points.title: Density
points.brief: Density is mass divided by volume. The volume of an irregular object can be found by how much water it displaces, and less dense objects float on denser liquids.

points.title: Solutes, solvents and solutions
points.brief: A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution. A substance that dissolves is soluble, and one that does not is insoluble.

points.title: Solubility and temperature
points.brief: Solubility is how much solute dissolves in a set amount of solvent. For most solids it rises as the water gets hotter.

points.title: Dilute, concentrated and saturated
points.brief: A dilute solution has little solute, a concentrated one has a lot, and a saturated one can dissolve no more at that temperature.

points.title: Pure substances and mixtures
points.brief: Elements and compounds are pure substances with one kind of particle. A mixture has different substances that are not chemically joined and can be separated.

points.title: Filtration
points.brief: Filtering separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, as in treating drinking water, and sieving and decanting work in a similar way.

points.title: Evaporation and crystallisation
points.brief: Heating a solution until the solvent evaporates leaves the dissolved solid behind, often as crystals, as in making salt from seawater.

points.title: Distillation
points.brief: Distillation boils a liquid and cools the vapour back into a liquid, separating it from dissolved solids or from liquids with different boiling points.

points.title: Chromatography
points.brief: Chromatography separates a mixture of dissolved substances, such as inks, because each travels a different distance up the paper with the solvent.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander separation methods
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have long used separation methods, such as grinding and sieving seeds and soaking and washing some seeds to remove toxins before eating.

points.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
points.brief: An atom is the smallest part of an element. Its nucleus holds positive protons and neutral neutrons, and negative electrons move around it.

points.title: Atomic number and electron shells
points.brief: The atomic number is the number of protons. In the first 18 elements, electrons fill shells around the nucleus, two in the first shell and up to eight in the next two.

points.title: Changing models of the atom
points.brief: Models of the atom changed as new experiments gave new evidence, from Dalton's solid ball to Thomson's, Rutherford's nucleus and Bohr's electron shells.

points.title: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
points.brief: Metals are shiny, conduct heat and electricity and can be bent. Most non-metals are dull and do not conduct. Metalloids are in between, and these properties decide how each is used.

points.title: Element symbols and compounds
points.brief: Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, and a formula such as H2O or CO2 shows which elements are joined in a compound.

points.title: Groups and periods
points.brief: Columns are groups of elements with similar properties and rows are periods. An element's place lets us predict its properties, such as how reactive it is.

points.title: Building the periodic table
points.brief: Mendeleev ordered the known elements by their properties and left gaps for elements not yet found, and later discoveries filled them.

points.title: Energy stores
points.brief: Energy can be stored as kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical and thermal energy.

points.title: Energy transfers
points.brief: Heat moves by conduction in solids, by convection in liquids and gases, and by radiation, which needs no matter, as when sunlight reaches Earth.

points.title: Energy transformations
points.brief: Energy changes from one form to another, such as chemical to kinetic in a car, and flow diagrams show the energy going in and coming out.

points.title: Conservation of energy
points.brief: Energy cannot be made or destroyed, only changed or moved. In an open system energy and matter can enter and leave, and in a closed system only energy can.

points.title: Physical and chemical change
points.brief: A physical change, such as melting, makes no new substance. A chemical change makes a new one, shown by signs such as a colour change, gas bubbles, light or a precipitate.

points.title: Word equations
points.brief: A word equation names the reactants on the left and the products on the right, such as magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide.

points.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
points.brief: Exothermic reactions give out heat and endothermic reactions take it in, which we can measure as a temperature change.

points.title: Photosynthesis and respiration
points.brief: In photosynthesis plants use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Respiration in cells uses glucose and oxygen to release energy.

points.title: Moving plates
points.brief: Earth's crust is broken into plates that move slowly. Where they pull apart, push together or slide past, they cause earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

points.title: Evidence for moving continents
points.brief: Wegener saw that coastlines fit together and matching fossils and rocks are found on distant continents. Later sea floor evidence turned his idea into plate tectonics.

points.title: Aboriginal accounts of volcanoes
points.brief: Some Aboriginal cultural accounts record volcanic activity, such as Gunditjmara accounts of Budj Bim in western Victoria, which match what geologists have found.

points.title: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
points.brief: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma, sedimentary rocks from layers of pressed sediment, and metamorphic rocks from rock changed by heat and pressure. Rocks are made of minerals.

points.title: The rock cycle
points.brief: Weathering, erosion, burial, heat, pressure and melting slowly turn one rock type into another in a cycle.

points.title: How fossils form
points.brief: A fossil forms when the remains or traces of a living thing are buried in sediment and slowly replaced by minerals, showing that different organisms lived at different times.

points.title: Relative dating of rock layers
points.brief: In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, the lowest layers are oldest, so fossils in lower layers are older than those above them.
